title: Python Mutable and Immutable Objects
learningObjectives: Define mutability in terms of whether an object can change in place.
Identify common mutable and immutable built-in types.
Distinguish mutation from rebinding a variable name.
Explain how multiple names can share a mutable object.
Choose copying or immutable values when shared changes would be undesirable.

understand.concept: A mutable object can be changed after it is created; an immutable object cannot be changed in place. Common mutable built-in types include list, dict and set. Common immutable types include int, float, bool, str and tuple. Assignment can create another name for the same object. If that object is mutable, an in-place change made through one name can be observed through the other. Rebinding one name does not change the binding of the other name.
understand.whyItMatters: Mutability is central to understanding collections, function arguments, shared state and bugs caused by unexpected side effects. Learners need to know when a change affects an existing object and when an operation creates a new value.
understand.analogy: Two people can hold references to the same shared whiteboard. If one person writes on it, both see the change. A printed page, by contrast, cannot be edited in place; a revised page must be created.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not describe Python's memory management. Also, a tuple is immutable as a container but may contain a mutable object whose contents can still change.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Mutable objects

Mutable objects support changes to their contents or state after creation. Examples include lists, dictionaries and sets. Methods such as `list.append()` and dictionary item assignment mutate the existing object.

## 2. Immutable objects

Immutable objects cannot be changed in place. Common examples include integers, floats, Booleans, strings and tuples. Operations that appear to change an immutable value instead produce a new object or a new result.

## 3. Aliasing and shared references

When `second = first` is executed, Python does not automatically create an independent copy of a mutable object. Both names can refer to the same object. Mutating it through either name is visible through both names.

## 4. Rebinding is different

If `first` is later assigned a new list, only the name first is rebound. The name second continues to refer to the original list. This differs from mutating the original list with append(), clear() or item assignment.

## 5. Copy when independent state is required

Use an appropriate copy operation when you need a separate collection. A shallow copy creates a new outer collection but still shares nested objects. Deep copying is a separate topic and should be used thoughtfully.

examples.title: Mutate a list through an alias
examples.explanation: Both names refer to the same list, so appending through other changes the list observed through items.

examples.title: Rebind a name instead of mutating
examples.code:
items = [1, 2]
other = items
items = [7, 8]
print(items)
print(other)
examples.explanation: The assignment creates a new list and rebinds items. other still refers to the original list.

examples.title: Strings are immutable
examples.explanation: upper() returns a new string. The original string object remains unchanged.

examples.title: Make a shallow list copy
examples.code:
original = [2, 4]
copy = original.copy()
copy.append(6)
print(original)
print(copy)
examples.explanation: copy() creates a new outer list, so appending to the copy does not change the original list.

examples.title: A tuple can contain a mutable object
examples.explanation: The tuple's element references cannot be reassigned, but the list referenced by its first element remains mutable.

practise.guidedTask: Create a list and assign it to two names. Append through the second name and observe the first. Then use copy() and repeat the operation.
practise.independentTask: Build a small program that stores a list of tasks. Demonstrate aliasing, rebinding and shallow copying, and write comments describing which operations mutate an existing object.
hints: Lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable.
Strings, numbers, Booleans and tuples are immutable containers/values.
Assignment does not automatically copy a mutable object.
append() mutates a list; assigning a new list rebinds a name.
A shallow copy does not recursively copy nested objects.
practise.challenge: Create a nested list, make a shallow copy, and demonstrate that the outer lists are separate while an inner list can still be shared. Explain when a deeper copy might be required.

questions.explanation: A list can be changed in place by adding, removing or replacing elements.

questions.prompt: What happens after second = first when first refers to a list?
options: Both names can refer to the same list object
A deep copy is always created
questions.answer: Both names can refer to the same list object
questions.explanation: Assignment binds another name to the existing object; it does not automatically copy the list.

questions.prompt: Which operation mutates a list in place?
questions.explanation: list.append() adds an element to the existing list object.

options: A shallow copy of the outer list
A deep copy of every nested object
A reference to a new dictionary
questions.answer: A shallow copy of the outer list
questions.explanation: The copied list is a new outer object, but nested objects may still be shared.

questions.prompt: Can a tuple contain a mutable list?
options: No, tuples can contain only immutable objects
Only if the list is empty
questions.explanation: A tuple cannot reassign its element references, but an object referenced by an element may itself be mutable.
